translation: She looks at the family, all girls, a mother with a child at her breast is clumsily getting off a cart and the driver rushes her because the cart needs to immediately return for others in the suburbs.
A bundle she had on her back falls and spills out some grayish rags and a single string of small, darkened beads.
The woman gathers them up feeling embarrassed as if she just exposed her deepest secrets to the world.
Deymowa passes by, and suddenly a boy of perhaps six or seven years runs up to her and looking at her with smiling eyes very pleased with himself says: "Praised be Jesus Christ!".
She responds automatically but solemnly: "Forever and ever, amen".
And now she clutches at her heart as tears well up in her eyes.
She kneels next to the boy, grabs him by his wrists; he continues looking into her tearful eyes still smiling what a charming little rascal.
The first buildings suddenly appear in front of them, without warning.
Apparently, the fog changes the sense of distance because Kaśka seems surprised by this too.
Suddenly she jumps, jerking on the shafts, and if it wasn't for Roszek's firm reaction and his whip, she would have overturned the carriage.
Perhaps
Kaśka was frightened by the sparks flying from the forge or maybe she picked up on anxiety from horses waiting for their turn to be shod.
Everywhere there is a sickly smell of malt, permeating every item for sale.
One could fill up on it as though it were bread.
On the outskirts of Rohatyn, in Babintsi, there are several small breweries from where this saturating scent difusses into the surrounding area.
Many market stalls sell beer here, and better shops stock both spirits and mead, especially ordinary mead.
The store owned by Jewish merchant Wakszul offers wine real Hungarian and Rhine wines along with slightly tart ones brought all the way from Wallachia.
The most to say would be about the Wołowski family, as it has grown to huge sizes.
Almost all branches of this family were ennobled some under the Bawół coat of arms, others under the Na Kaskach coat of arms.
Without a doubt, Franciszek made a great career he was the son of Izaak Wołowski, who was called Jeremiah by priest Chmielowski.
He was born in 1786 in Brünn and raised in Offenbach and became one of the best lawyers and experts on law at that time.

Interestingly, when a proposal appeared in parliament to grant Polish citizenship to Jews, Franciszek as a member of parliament argued in his impassioned speech that it is not yet time for such action.
First the Polish nation must gain independence and then there will be time for social reforms.
All the Neophytes of Offenbach were buried in the city cemetery, which after years began to hinder the city's expansion plans and was closed down in 1866.
The bones of those buried there were collected and respectfully reburied elsewhere.
On this occasion, Jakub Frank's skull was exhumed from his grave and, meticulously labelled as "the skull of a Jewish patriarch," it ended up in the hands of the Offenbach city historian.
Many years later, under unknown circumstances, it found its way to Berlin where it underwent detailed measurements and analysis and was deemed an example of Jewish racial inferiority.
After the war, it vanished without trace perhaps destroyed in wartime chaos or reduced to dust or may still lie within an underground archive somewhere in a museum.
After Jakub's death, a time of great tranquility came for me.
My main occupation became studying the Merkavah, to which were added our conversations with Jeruchim Dembowski, as we lived in the same room, bringing us closer to each other.
I also told him about Chai Szor she was the only woman I could love and I loved her from that beautiful moment when I got her for one night, when I brought news about Jakub to Rohatyn.
But above all, I loved Jakub.
They had been in Ivania since April.
If not for the good people of Ivania, they probably would have starved to death.
Ivania saved their lives and health;
Bejla is feeling better now and she doesn't cough as much.
Srol believes that once they are baptized, they will be doing just as well as the Christians.
They will get a piece of land, Bejla will have vegetables in her garden, and he, Srol, will weave kilims because he is good at it.
In old age when they marry off their daughters, those daughters will take them in.
These are all his dreams.
"Look, good sir, Kaśka does not want to go," Roszko says grimly as the carriage comes to a halt.
Roszko dismounts from the mount and a few times bids farewell excessively.
Then he leans over and peers into the fog, as if looking at water.
A shirt comes out from under his holiday red coat, though it is already somewhat faded.
"I don't know where to go," he says.
"How do you not know?
We're already on the Rohatyn highway," says the priest in surprise.
Yet!
He gets out of the carriage and follows his servant aimlessly around it, straining his eyes into white nothingness.
They think they see something but their eyes begin to play tricks when they can't latch onto anything solid .
What an odd predicament!
It's like getting lost in one's own pocket.
"Quiet!" suddenly says the priest and raising his finger up listening intently .
And indeed , somewhere on left side among clouds of fog we hear a faint sound of streaming water .
"Let us follow that noise .
It must be running water , " decides priest.
Soon the priest relaxes into the carriage, stretches out his legs and allows his eyes to wander over the sea of mist.
He immediately falls into a travel reverie, for a man thinks best when in motion.

Slowly, hesitantly his mind's mechanism springs to life, gears and cogs meshing together like in a clock he owns that sits in his presbytery corridor which was bought in Lviv; he paid handsomely for it.
In no time it would chime 'bim-bom'.
He starts to wonder if perhaps the world didn't come from such mist.
After all, Jewish historian Josephus maintains that the world was created in autumn during equinoctium autumnale .
One can assume so as there were fruits present in Eden; since an apple hung on the tree it must have been Autumn.
There is some truth there.
But soon another thought comes:
What kind of argument is this?
Couldn't an almighty God create such petty fruits extra, at any time of year?
When they reach the main road leading to Rohatyn, they join the stream of pedestrians, horsemen and every kind of wagon emerging from the fog, as if baked out of bread for Christmas.
It's Wednesday, market day in Rohatyn; peasant wagons laden with sacks of grain, cages full of poultry and all manner of agricultural produce pass by.
Among them march traders carrying a variety of goods; their cleverly folded stalls are carried on their backs like yokes.
In a moment they'll have tables spread with colorful fabrics, wooden toys and eggs bought cheaply from villagers.
Peasants also lead goats and cows to sell at the market animals terrified by all the clamor resist and balk in puddles.
They are passed by a fast-moving cart covered with a tattered tarpaulin full of raucous Jews from surrounding areas heading into Rohatyn for market day.

Closely following behind is an elegant coach that struggles to maintain its dignity amid all this foggy traffic; its highly polished doors have been blackened by mud and its coachman wearing a blue cloak looks confused evidently he did not expect such chaos as now he desperately scans for an opportunity to exit this devilish road.
